World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

Shamsuddoza Sajen is a journalist and researcher. He can be contacted at [email protected].

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: The RBA's post-COVID rate hikes caused Australians to work more
World.content:
Now that the Reserve Bank has lifted interest rates for the third time this year, how will you respond?

Are you thinking about getting a second or third job, or entering the workforce, to pay for your household's rising interest payments?

Because a recent working paper published by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) found that this is exactly what thousands of Australians did when the RBA hiked rates rapidly in 2022 and 2023.

Reserve Bank lifts interest rates by 0.25pc, to 4.35pc The RBA has lifted rates by 0.25 basis points to 4.35 per cent, which fully unwind last year's rate cuts.

It found that it led to an increase in the supply of labour in Australia that was so significant that it challenged a long-held central bank idea.

As the paper explained, a common working assumption for central banks is that labour supply is not significantly affected by monetary policy.

As the thinking goes, when central banks lift interest rates, the higher rates increase firms' borrowing costs, which, in turn, reduces investment, output, and employment. So, tighter monetary policy impacts labour markets indirectly through firms' demand for labour.

But the paper found that this is not what happened in Australia in 2022-23.

It said that when the RBA lifted rates rapidly, many Australians in highly indebted households entered the workforce (if they were not already working), or took on second or third jobs, or increased their hours, in a pronounced way.

"We have tested and rejected the hypothesis that labour supply is unresponsive to monetary policy settings," the paper said.

Most Australian mortgages are floating-rate

The paper's authors are Mitali Das, Jonathan Hambur, Klaus-Peter Hellwig, and John Spray.

Jonathan Hambur is an RBA economist, but the paper represents his personal views, not those of the bank.

They studied the period of monetary policy tightening that began in Australia in May 2022 and ran their analysis through to June 2025 (the RBA started cutting rates again in February 2025). During that time, the RBA increased the cash rate target by a cumulative 4.25 percentage points over 13 consecutive rate hikes.

"The scale and speed of this episode provide an unusually sharp and well-defined shift in monetary conditions, creating an ideal quasi-experiment to assess the effects of monetary policy tightening on household behaviour," their paper says.

In the graph below, the black line shows the RBA's rapid rate hikes from mid-2022, compared to other RBA rate-hiking cycles.

(IMF Working Paper, "Labor Supply Effects of Monetary Policy: Evidence from Australian Mortgage Holders," prepared by Mitali Das, Jonathan Hambur, Klaus-Peter Hellwig & John Spray, April 2026.)

The paper says the transmission from monetary policy to mortgage holders happens very quickly in Australia.

That is because the share of households with variable-rate mortgages (typically indexed to the RBA's policy cash rate) is substantially higher than in other advanced economies, accounting for around 70 per cent of outstanding mortgages in 2022, compared with less than 20 per cent in the United Kingdom and under 5 per cent in the United States.

More Aussies working two or more jobs More people than ever before are picking up multiple jobs as the high cost of living pushes Australians to take on extra work, but the tax office warns people not to get caught out and know their obligations.

That combination of a high prevalence of variable-rate borrowing and elevated household debt levels in Australia implies that interest rate changes can generate large and immediate effects on household cash flows in Australia.

The paper also notes that the RBA's rapid rate hikes occurred against a backdrop of an unusually strong labour market when unemployment was near multi-decade lows, and labour demand (from businesses) was elevated relative to historical tightening cycles.

That suggests that the ability for Australians to increase their supply of labour partly reflected strong underlying labour demand.

Overall, the paper shows that the labour supply response to higher interest rates was significant in Australia.

"The share of individuals working more than one job in Australia increased by 0.4 percentage points since the beginning of the rate-hiking cycle, which was equivalent to more than 100,000 additional workers," it found.

The graph below shows when the multiple job-holding rate jumped well above its long-term trend.

(IMF Working Paper, "Labor Supply Effects of Monetary Policy: Evidence from Australian Mortgage Holders," prepared by Mitali Das, Jonathan Hambur, Klaus-Peter Hellwig & John Spray, April 2026.)

"Meanwhile, the participation rate has reached an historic high of 67 per cent, up from its pre-COVID level of roughly 66 per cent," the paper says.

Natural experiment: Interest rates and childcare

The paper found that the increase in interest rates in Australia induced a labour supply response among households most exposed to rising debt servicing costs.

It did not find a larger labour supply response from renters.

"Unlike mortgage holders, renters are not directly exposed to increases in mortgage interest costs but are fully exposed to changes in the cost of living," it says. "Across all outcomes and periods, we find no differential labour supply response among renters."

It also found that members of highly indebted households responded specifically to rising interest rates, not rising inflation.

And the effects were strongest among those without children. Highly indebted workers with children exhibited small (or even zero) labour supply responses to tightening interest rates.

Child care subsidies are increasing — Here's what you need to know From today, about 1.2 million Australian families are in line for a childcare rebate boost. Here's what the new federal government changes could mean for you.

However, it also found that when rising childcare costs became a national concern in Australia in 2022, which prompted the federal government to increase childcare subsidies from July 2023 onwards, this provided a "quasi-experiment setting" to examine how labour supply would respond.

And it found that, in response to those childcare subsidy reforms, there was a notable increase in the probability of employment, and a notable increase in the number of jobs per 100 workers, for individuals with young children, relative to those with no children.

In the graph below, see the light-blue line.

(IMF Working Paper, "Labor Supply Effects of Monetary Policy: Evidence from Australian Mortgage Holders," prepared by Mitali Das, Jonathan Hambur, Klaus-Peter Hellwig & John Spray, April 2026.)

The authors said in the context of their paper that Australia's childcare subsidies were a clear illustration of fiscal-monetary policy interaction in determining the supply of labour.

Challenges a long-held assumption

In all, the paper says macro-economic models largely preclude a labour supply response to monetary policy shocks, and that view of monetary policy is reflected in explicit statements by major central banks.

For example, in its February 2024 quarterly statement on monetary policy, the Reserve Bank of Australia commented:

"Monetary policy has little direct effect on labour supply or structural features of the job market, and so generally takes the current level of full employment as given."

But, the paper says, a small number of recent papers have started to question that assumption, arguing that rising interest rates can lead to increased supply of labour.

"If this is the case, it has important implications for both the interpretation and forecasting of macroeconomic conditions, as well as for our understanding of the transmission of monetary policy," it says.

"An increase in labour supply following an interest rate hike would dampen the effect of contractionary policy on output, while potentially amplifying its effect on inflation through downward pressure on wages and, in turn, prices.

"Moreover, such responses may have distributional and welfare consequences, particularly if the labour supply response is more evident among certain household types," it says.

It reminds people that the results are derived from the specific context of post-COVID Australia, but it says they still hold lessons for advanced economies more generally, notably countries where variable-rate mortgages are more prevalent.

So, now that the RBA has lifted rates for the third time this year, how are you planning to pay for your household's rising interest payments?

World.title: Councils to get federal funds for roads, pipes and wires in housing push
World.content:
Local councils will get federal money to build roads, pipes and wires to enable new housing in an effort to signal the Albanese government remains determined to boost supply despite its flagging 1.2 million homes target and its pivot to housing tax hikes.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers will reveal details of the $2 billion fund in Tuesday's federal budget, declaring the cash injection will add an extra 65,000 homes over a decade.

The policy echoes a promise made by Peter Dutton in last year's election campaign to devote federal resources to the so-called "enabling infrastructure" which councils are often left to bankroll themselves, often in negotiation with developers.

Whereas Mr Dutton's plan was targeted at outer suburban "greenfield" housing, this new program is less specific and will also flow to state utility companies, adding to $1 billion the federal government gave state governments for a similar purpose in the last term.

Some people will hate Tuesday's federal budget but Jim Chalmers doesn't mind For once, the budget won't be a dull one. Jim Chalmers's tax reforms will create a stir and some question whether they will close the generation gap, but the treasurer is projecting a relaxed figure.

The centrepiece of Mr Chalmers' fifth budget will be contentious changes to the capital gains tax and negative gearing, sold to voters an effort to fight generational disadvantage in the housing market.

An important policy detail will be whether Labor chooses to spare those who invest in newly-built homes from its higher tax regime, since economists warn the tax reform could otherwise slightly dampen construction.

"Building more homes is a big focus of this budget," Mr Chalmers said.

"Our housing plan is pro-aspiration and it's pro-investment.

"We're coming at this housing challenge from every responsible angle and boosting supply is central to that."

Further steps to cut housing red tape

Housing Minister Clare O'Neil said infrastructure was "the boring but essential work that unlocks housing supply", setting up water, power, sewerage and access roads for "new homes and new communities", with $500 million reserved for the regions.

Housing Minister Clare O'Neil says this infrastructure was "boring but essential work". (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

It is unclear whether the $2 billion, badged as a Local Infrastructure Fund, will come directly out of the budget or be funnelled through an investment vehicle, a model Labor has often used for housing policy.

The federal budget will also include a pledge to make it free for construction companies to access mandatory Australian regulatory standards in a move the government says will save small firms up to $1,600.

There will also be further steps to cut housing red tape in conjunction with state governments, including an effort to encourage so-called "modern methods of construction" such as modular homes.

Australia's construction sector is less efficient now than it was in the 1990s, and despite some signs of an uptick in housing approvals since Labor's 1.2 million homes target began, the current trajectory is just shy of 1 million over the target's five years.

Loading...

The Middle East war is expected to deal another blow to the construction sector which relies on fuel and also oil-derived products such as plastic pipes.

The Coalition's 2025 election policy for enabling infrastructure was a $5 billion fund it said could deliver 500,000 new homes, although this was a rough approximation produced by developer lobby group UDIA, which simply assumed $10,000 per home.

Last year, Liverpool mayor Ned Mannoun told the ABC he supported that policy and that federal intervention was "definitely needed", saying the $1.7 billion of new housing in his local government area in 2024 could have been much greater with more infrastructure.

But Naim Kurt, the mayor of Hume in Melbourne's north-west, said money for arterial roads was more urgently needed because the rapid expansion of the city's urban fringe meant that, even if infrastructure could be provided, traffic into the city was intolerable.

World.title: Want to cross the Strait of Hormuz? Email the IRGC
World.content:
Iran has launched what it calls the Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA), seemingly to govern over the Strait of Hormuz — the vital shipping choke point the regime is now claiming as its own.

Through the authority, ship captains and operators can apply directly to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) for permission to cross the Strait of Hormuz.

The so-called PGSA even provides an email address where applications can be made.

We sent a request to the address asking for the regime's rules and regulations for the Strait of Hormuz.

And the IRGC got back to us.

Iran war live updates: For the latest news on the Middle East crisis, read our blog.

IRGC's new system to exit strait

We were sent an application in the form of an Excel spreadsheet and instructions to fill it out, submit it for a "compliance review" and await further instructions.

"Following your request for passage through the Hormuz Strait, you are required to complete all requested information in the attached file in full. Submission of complete and accurate information is essential and will ensure the timely processing of your request," the email read.

The so-called Persian Gulf Strait Authority sent the ABC this form, which appears to be designed as an application for ships to cross the Strait of Hormuz. (Supplied: IRGC)

The Excel spreadsheet asks for the name of the vessel, along with more than 40 other data points including the type and value of the cargo, the current and previous flags of the ship, the nationalities of the owner and operators, and whether the applicant seeks to travel east or west.

The move appears to be another attempt by the IRGC to formalise its control over the Strait of Hormuz — a narrow body of water it shares with Oman and through which 20 per cent of global oil and gas shipments usually pass.

Since the early days of the war Iran has effectively closed the waterway, trapping most Gulf nations' oil in the Persian Gulf and prompting a global fuel crisis.

A senior analyst with maritime intelligence company Windward, Michelle Bockmann, told the ABC that traffic in the strait had dwindled since the US began a naval blockade of Iran nearly four weeks ago.

Some nations, including Pakistan and India, have reportedly negotiated the safe passage of ships destined for their ports.

There is some reporting that Iran has been charging a toll on some ships willing to pay it.

The ships that have been engaging with Iran's so-called "toll booth" are navigated to the north of the Strait of Hormuz and around the country's Larak Island before sailing towards the Gulf of Oman and beyond.

Now, with the establishment of the PGSA and the release of a new Iranian map of the Strait of Hormuz, it appears Iran is trying to further sell the idea that it owns and administers the waterway.

"I don't necessarily think that Iran believes that they're going to be able to affect a toll booth system," said Obsidian Risk Advisors sanctions specialist Brett Erickson.

" I think it's primarily setting the stage to the world that one way or another, Iran is going to get paid here. "

Jennifer Parker, a former naval officer with experience in the Middle East, said this was "all about trying to exert control".

"Iran has said for quite a while now that ships that wish to transit the strait must do so through the transit route that Iran has outlined," she said.

In a new map of the region released through Iranian state media, the Strait of Hormuz extends much further east into the Persian Gulf and further west into the Gulf of Oman, which would include key ports and oil terminals typically accessed without entering the strait.

The regime said these were the "new boundaries of the Strait of Hormuz" that would be controlled by its armed forces.

Iran's new map of the Strait of Hormuz extends the waterway's boundaries much further to the east and west. (Supplied: Consulate General of the Islamic Republic of Iran- Hyderabad/Fars News Agency)

The map and application form might look official, but global sanctions on Iran, as well as terrorist financing legislation, means few countries would be legally able to engage with them if payment was sought.

"It is not just in violation of US sanctions," Mr Erickson said.

"It is in violation of UK sanctions, EU sanctions, Canadian sanctions, and Australian sanctions to make payments to Iran or the IRGC."

Mr Erickson said unwinding sanctions, or lifting laws designed to prevent cash from making its way to designated terrorist organisations, would be unlikely and also take more time than the United States had in its current negotiating posture.

And all of this is happening while the Trump administration has been changing course on its own strategy in the strait.

The situation leaves ship owners and captains with less certainty about when they might be able to safely sail.

Conflicting messages in the strait

After the first round of negotiations for a peace deal in Islamabad, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi announced the Strait of Hormuz had been opened, and some ships attempted to make their break.

But the IRGC quickly flexed its muscle and closed it.

His team claimed Project Freedom was working. Then Trump put it on hold Iran branded Project Freedom as "Project Deadlock". Now the operation is on hold.

Then, US President Donald Trump announced Project Freedom, an operation with vague scope and communication that promised to guide ships through the Strait of Hormuz.

But Mr Erickson said where ship captains and operators might have been willing to attempt a crossing at the first sign of opening, the weeks since had led to confusion and caution.

"The last time we heard the strait is open vessels got shot at," he said.

He said any time there was an attack on a vessel it was possible to watch on marine tracker software as groups of ships performed a "U-turn" and aborted any attempted crossing.

Iran's foreign minister announced the strait was open on April 17. But the IRGC quickly slammed it shut. (Kpler Marine Traffic/ABC News: Linday Dunbar)

"Who really wants to be the first mover right now on anything that is operating essentially on just the United States's word that it's safe?" Mr Erickson said.

Some ships did attempt to leave the strait during Project Freedom. The White House was quick to report two US-flagged merchant ships were guided out of the strait.

However, on Wednesday, the French cargo ship San Antonio was hit.

Injured members of its crew were evacuated for medical treatment, according to Reuters. And the NYT reported the French vessel was following input from the US Navy as part of the now-paused Project Freedom.

It is another example of ships stuck in the strait trying to make sense of information being put out by the US and Iran alike.

At times, the information is changing faster than the literal tides.

"Every time that something like that happens it makes the process to resumption of normal traffic even that more extended," Mr Erickson said.

"Vessels are seeing over and over again how quickly this can unravel and the cost and risk to their captain and crews' lives."

In the Strait of Hormuz, Iran unleashes a plot years in the making By moving so much of the war into the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf, Tehran has hit its adversaries where it hurts the most.

In another confusing moment, Secretary of State Marco Rubio faced reporters on Wednesday in the White House and declared the US operation in Iran was "over".

He explained the war was done and now the focus was on a completely different American effort — Project Freedom.

It was touted as a way to provide "humanitarian support" for stranded ships and crews.

Hours later the US president announced on Truth Social the day-old project would also be "paused".

"I was surprised to see the US cancel that," Ms Parker said.

According to her, the idea had limitations, but "at least you would be able to allow some of the 2,000 vessels trapped in the strait to escape".

"I think that has probably undermined some of their position on the Strait of Hormuz and trust with mariners in the region," she said.

"We will have to see whether the negotiations or the peace deal that has been touted as the reason it was cancelled do come to fruition."

Stuck at the strait

Trump has yet again recently played up the prospects of an agreement.

While there were many sticking points for both sides, the Strait of Hormuz has emerged as a crucial one said Ali Mamouri, an expert in Middle East studies and research fellow at Deakin University.

"Both parties want to open the waterway but they want to do it in a way that doesn't show that they lost," he said.

"All the goals that Donald Trump announced at the beginning of the war, none of them happened on the ground."

Iran and US in 'game of chicken' There are duelling narratives from Iran and the US about the economic pressures of the war, so will the blockade get negotiations going?

Dr Mamouri said the situation since February had made Iran somewhat stronger.

"In addition to their traditional powers, their regional allies and missiles program, and nuclear, now they have Hormuz as well," he said.

While there are many reasons for the US president to want this war to end — for example, his dipping domestic popularity and rising costs for Americans — Dr Mamouri wonders if something far from home is giving Trump a peace deal deadline.

"It seems to me the US president is willing to get to some kind of a solution for this crisis before his trip to China," he said.

But, he said: "Iranians are not willing to get to any kind of a deal, under any pressure."

World.title: Big Brother's 25-year journey from raunchy nudity to 'family friendly'
World.content:
Welcome to Cheat Sheet, where we give you all the intel you need about iconic shows! In honour of its 25th birthday and the recent announcement of a 2026 season, this month we’re looking at landmark reality TV show Big Brother Australia.

When Channel 10's Big Brother reboot soft launched onto Australian screens at the end of 2025, the approach was short, sharp and maximised to reach the most eyes possible.

Instead of being confined to a television broadcast or the network's website, the month-long season would be beamed across social media platforms — including a 24-hour stream on TikTok.

The 2025 Big Brother Australia contestants spent a month together in a house, while 2000s editions went for as long as three months. (Instagram: @bigbrotherau)

After being tossed around networks for more than a decade, producers Endemol Shine and returning broadcaster Channel 10/Paramount were focused on "total digital saturation".

"It had to be unmissable; this is TV that you couldn't escape. It didn't matter where you were, you would always find Big Brother," Paramount Unscripted head Sarah Thornton said at last month's Screen Forever conference.

Five months down the track, the strategy has proved a hit. Broadcast numbers are the highest they've been since 2021, with Paramount boasting the series provided 449 million minutes of streaming.

Twenty-five years since the format hit Australian shores, and with a 2026 season confirmed, let's look back at the journey of Big Brother Australia.

The history of Big Brother Australia

The Big Brother franchise was imported from the Netherlands where, in 1999, media master John de Mol Jr conceptualised a show where 'housemates' would be monitored around the clock; when they relaxed, when they slept, when they showered.

Taking its name from the omnipotent antagonist from George Orwell's 1984, housemates would engage in various tasks and games in pursuit of a cash prize.

The Big Brother eye logo has gone through multiple re-designs but remains an iconic image of the series. (YouTube: @bigbrotherau)

But in addition to playing literal games, housemates would also have to play a social game in order to avoid intra-house 'nomination' — a one-way ticket to public-voted elimination and a swift exit from the house.

Syndicated to Australia in 2001, the concept of voluntary 24-hour surveillance as a form of entertainment was so foreign that broadcaster Channel 10 explained it to potential viewers by comparing it to the 1998 movie The Truman Show, which featured a man (played by Jim Carrey) filmed from birth in an artificial town and broadcast to a public audience as prime-time viewing.

More than 9,000 people applied to appear on the inaugural season of Big Brother Australia, enticed not only by the $250,000 prize money ($477,901 in today's value) but at the prospect of becoming "a new type of celebrity".

While the whittled-down 120 hopefuls faced casting directors and psychologists, the house in which the lucky few would reside was being built at Gold Coast theme park Dreamworld.

Riddled with double-sided mirrors, cameras and recording equipment, production designer Michael Bridges said the intention was for the audience to feel like "a voyeur, like you're peeking in on these people."

Then-Labor leader Mark Latham peers through the glass in the "camera run" area during a tour of the Big Brother house on the Gold Coast in 2004. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

The first season of Big Brother Australia also had a digital element, which was cutting edge for 2001. But rather than rolling 24-hour footage beamed directly into their pockets, fans could 

Big Brother Australia was a resounding success, with more than 1 million Australians tuning in per episode to watch housemates survive on chickpeas, manipulate the game, and bicker while baking their own bread.

More than 2.6 million fans watched the season finale to see Ben Williams crowned the first winner of Big Brother Australia.

As promised, the housemates of Big Brother became their own type of celebrity, appearing on multiple game shows across networks, releasing a single together on the official Big Brother compilation CD and contestant Sara-Marie Fedele becoming a household sensation for her signature 'bum dance'.

It was less than 12 months before Big Brother Australia season two beamed into TVs around the country. A compilation of footage from the first season is now a part of the National Film and Sound Archive.

The Big Brother house on the Gold Coast was redecorated every season. (YouTube: @bigbrotherau)

The impact of Big Brother Australia

Channel 10's first run with Big Brother extended for eight more seasons (plus a celebrity edition) to 2008 with the 2000's iterations being defined by their liberal approach to sex and nudity on screen.

Weekly episodes of Big Brother Uncut, a late night MA15+ version of the show, frequently showed various levels of nudity from the housemates, as well as housemate fraternisation and incidents too sexual to show during the daily show's PG time slot.

By the 2005 season, an Australian Communications and Media Authority investigation into three Uncut episodes found Channel 10 breached industry code of practice for broadcasting incidents such as a male housemate exposing his penis while massaging the shoulder of a female housemate, and a heavily sexual improvised song by some male housemates.

In response to the findings, Channel 10 issued an apology for any offence caused "… regarding the attitude of some male Big Brother housemates towards women".

Camilla Severi with Gretel Killeen at the 2006 Big Brother finale where the contestant came runner-up to Jamie Brooksby. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

The issue came to a head during the 2006 season where 20-year-old Michael "Ashley" Cox and Michael "John" Bric, 21 were expelled from the house mid-season after one man held down Camilla Severi, 22, and the other pushed his crotch into her face, in what was informally referred to as a " turkey slap". The footage was not shown on television broadcast but was picked up and disseminated by the online live stream.

Channel 10 released an interview with the accused pair downplaying the incident as a "practical joke". The network also broadcast Big Brother telling housemates of the pair's expulsion while Severi cried and apologised profusely, as well as a Diary Room interview where she backed up the assertion that it was a joke, but conceded that it "went too far".

In a 2020 interview, Severi said the scrutiny and attention the incident received at the time was a "confusing experience".

" I didn't ask for that to happen and sometimes when people ask me about it I say 'well, it's really interesting this keeps following me around because I didn't do it'. But am I scarred by it? No. "

While Queensland police spoke to parties involved, they concluded there was "insufficient evidence" for criminal charges.

Among a sea of backlash, then-Prime Minister John Howard called for Big Brother's cancellation.

"Here's a great opportunity for Channel 10 to do a bit of self-regulation and get this stupid program off the air," he said.

In response, Channel 10 cancelled its 'Adults Only' broadcast while asserting confidence the station had complied with industry codes.

The controversy saw Big Brother's seventh season debut to the smallest audience since its premiere, with commentators calling the season boring. Despite season eight replacing long-time host Gretel Killeen with radio shock jocks Kyle Sandilands and Jackie O and splashing out on stunts like having Pamala Anderson enter the house, ratings continued to nose dive.

Kyle Sandilands and Jackie O as Big Brother hosts in 2008. ( AAP: Southern Star/David Brown, file photo)

Shortly after the conclusion of season eight, Channel 10 officially cancelled Big Brother with then-chief programmer David Mott admitting the show had been struggling with "audience erosion".

Revived and rebooted

In 2012, Big Brother was revived for a ninth season, with new broadcaster Nine installing daytime TV star Sonia Kruger as host and switching to a 7pm time slot in order to cast off the raunch of previous seasons and make the show appear more "family friendly".

Sonia Kruger won the Gold Logie in 2023 in part for her hosting duties for Big Brother. (Supplied)

While the 2012 edition enjoyed viewership not seen since the third season, ratings quickly dropped in 2013, and even further in 2014. The following year Nine insisted Big Brother wasn't dead, despite the Dreamworld house being dismantled. Nine ultimately decided not to renew its partnership with Big Brother.

By 2020, it was time for Seven to have their crack at the format while making several dramatic changes. The twelfth season saw filming move from original Dreamworld house — which had been vandalised and burnt down — to Sydney.

Fights, sex, deaths and glitter: The rocky road to Euphoria season three Sam Levinson's controversial teen series has had to overcome four years of actor deaths, character departures and on-set tension to make it to season three.

Public voting was eliminated for everything but the grand finale, and the season marked the first time the show was pre-recorded (bar the grand finale).

Like Nine's reboot, Seven's iteration enjoyed an initial resurgence of audience interest only for viewership to fall dramatically over subsequent seasons. The season 15 finale, which was criticised by fans for changing the format to more closely resemble a dating game, captured just 152,000 viewers, with a repeat of Seven's Border Security more than doubling the finale's numbers.

Big Brother Australia did not return to Seven in 2024.

In late 2024, Ten announced at their upfronts that Big Brother Australia would return to its original network and format including the Dreamworld filming location, live evictions, public voting and 24-hour streaming.

The truncated 2025 season was praised as a return to form, climbing back to pre-2020 ratings.

Three landmark Big Brother moments

Dancing doona

In a sign of what would become Big Brother Australia's calling card, one of the moments that wormed its way into BB history was the tryst between season one's Pete Timbs and Christina Davis. The first housemates to couple up were caught on the Uncut cameras canoodling beneath an undulating blanket. Of course, it's never been confirmed what Pete and Christina were getting up to under there but the shock to 2001 audiences was enough for 'dancing doona' to enter the Australian pop-culture lexicon.

'Free th refugees'

The 'e' had become unstuck in Merlin Luck's otherwise impactful message. (Youtube: Channel 10)

Throughout the show's original Channel 10 run, evicted housemates were bundled from the house to a stage in front of a live audience to banter with Gretel Killeen. Despite strictly enforced rules on forbidden contraband, 2004 contestant Merlin Luck smuggled a sign reading "free th [sic] refugees" and a piece of black tape, which he revealed at his eviction interview, refusing to speak to an increasingly irate Killeen in silent protest of Australia's mandatory detention of asylum seekers.

$1 million and a wedding ring

Butler proposed to his then-girlfriend after winning $1 million as the Big Brother season four champion. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

In 2025, housemates were playing for $100,000 prize money, just a tenth of what was up for grabs in season four which promised the winner $1 million ($1.7 million in today's terms). So it's no surprise that when S4 housemate Trevor Butler took out the top prize, he turned around and proposed to his then-girlfriend Breea Forrest right on the Big Brother stage. She said yes, of course. The couple recently celebrated their 21st anniversary alongside their two children.

World.title: New exhibition charts motherhood from the 15th century to today
World.content:
Primal and glorious. Expected but unsupported. Nag and nurse.

Motherhood is often cast in contradictions, so it makes sense the new National Gallery of Victoria (NGV) exhibition Mother welcomes visitors with a contrasting pair of images.

Front and centre of the entrance to the space upstairs at Ian Potter Centre is a 15th-century oil painting of Madonna and Child by Giovanni Toscani and right next to it, a 1998 conical birth mat by East Arnhem Land artist Elizabeth Birritjama Ngalandjarri.

"It's such an amazing opportunity to bring things together that have never been shown in the same context before" says co-curator Sophie Gerhard, herself a mother.

"We see the Virgin Mary in her white, beautiful purity. But then we ask what impact did that have on women's bodies and birthing practises when Christianity came to Australia? They are lovely works, but also bigger conversations," she says.

The entrance to the exhibition provides visitors with seemingly contrasting images of mothering, which still share a universal thread. (Supplied)

Much like previous shows like Queer in 2022 and Cats and Dogs in 2025, Mother is curated almost entirely from the NGV's existing collection. It traverses the "life cycle" of a mother, from matrescence (the transition to motherhood) through to the giving of care, making of magic and and on to loss and grief.

First Nations mothering for generations

Telling the story of motherhood through the NGV collection has given the exhibition a distinctly local framing.

"There's been a few exhibitions on motherhood launched overseas and we were thinking about that in an NGV context and what we could add. We saw a real opportunity, especially in the light of these other shows overseas which did not have any kind of First Nation stories included," says co-curator Katharina Prugger, who was pregnant during the creation of the show.

Among the few new acquisitions is a work by Melbourne artist Kate Just.

A finely knitted chain mail armour for her adopted child Harper is called An Armour of Hope (2012), and captures both the fears and hopes when a mother is born, however she comes into it.

Kate Just's An Armour Of Hope is a symbol of maternal protection. (Supplied)

In an email to Prugger last year Just wrote: "The work An Armour of Hope strangely began the day I met Harper and shook his hand as a two-year-old joining our family for the first time.

"In that moment, I felt and saw an image of Harper in soft armour in my mind's eye. I think I recognised the difficulty Harper had already been through, but also noted a keen receptivity to new connections and bonds."

Fibre arts and textiles are threaded throughout the show — no surprise when you consider the overlapping worlds of craft and motherhood.

Take, for example, Quandamooka artist Kyra Mancktelow's work One Continuous String (2021).

G'ua G'ua, Erub, Mer woman Destiny Deacon used photos and videos in her work to break down Indigenous tropes and stereotypes. (Supplied: National Gallery of Victoria, purchased from the Estate of Destiny Deacon)

Mancktelow took the pattern of a cotton dress her grandmother was forced to wear at Moongalba (Myora mission) and made a replica using her grandmother's weaving technique.

Other prominent First Nations contributions to the show come from the late great Destiny Deacon whose 1987 work Home Video playfully subverts the trope of a bad Black mother, and Hannah Brontë's Eye Hear U Magik, which pays homage to intergenerational spiritual knowledge.

Who is a mother?

From Davida Allen's witty 1989 lithograph Baby to John Lorimer's oil painting of a 17th-century colonial maid of colour tending to a white child, there are hugely varying experiences of motherhood to see and feel through the show.

Davida Allen, whose 1989 lithograph Baby is part of the exhibition, has created numerous works centred around the concept of family. (Supplied)

Birth, nursing, drudgery, longing and play all find expression here.

Photography and video are also prominent throughout.

These realistic glimpses have become essential parts of domestic life, making invisible work visible and capturing how warped time can feel in families.

An earthenware feeding bottle from Staffordshire in 1850 is displayed alongside vintage and antique prams, toys and clothing.

Does the show capture every facet of motherhood? No show could, especially one that relies so heavily on existing collections.

Loading...

There are also some omissions of how we parent now — IVF didn't seem hugely visible, for example.

It's hard not to imagine a different show had the budget been stretched to include more new acquisitions.

But, as Gerhard says, it is a meaningful show for so many.

"It's been amazing to develop something where the work is really so relevant to people's lives," she says.

"Usually work in contemporary art, you're looking at something with political significance or things like that. But this has just been such a different experience in terms of the feedback we were already getting and excitement around it, even, just people from our lives."

Prugger adds: "This show seems to make people want to share. Every person that we've walked through says 'oh, this reminds me of my family'."

The exhibition is a nod to many facets of motherhood, but cannot, through the sheer spectrum of experiences, touch on them all.

But the exhibition doesn't satisfy itself with the personal, thrumming throughout with the political.

It consistently asks us to consider maternal aesthetics more deeply: which images reinforce tight and unrelenting roles of mother and which give carers more room to be fully realised humans? How could art ever reflect the immensity of the task that is being a mother?

As someone currently on maternity leave, writing this piece with a squirming infant on my lap, it was a relief to see a grand venue such as the Ian Potter Centre give itself over to these questions — and to see how the long thread that connects all mothers could be woven in this time and place.

Mother is at the NGV until July 12.

World.title: We're living in the age of exhaustion. Who pays the price of burnout?
World.content:
For years workers were taught to endure stress in silence. Now, rising burnout is forcing employers and governments to confront the cost of modern work.

Hayley Hughes said yes to everything. She worked in health care at a Queensland medical centre, managing nine GPs and up to 18 staff, while overseeing a change of ownership.

"I kept delivering," she says. "It took over my life."

The increased pace of her work meant that she was never "off".

"My phone didn't stop and I really struggled to step away from the task list," Hayley says.

Over many months of an intense workload, Hayley started to feel physically ill from the stress. She experienced brain fog, a racing heart and insomnia.

Jeffrey Smith was working as a senior lawyer for an insurance company in Sydney as the business was collapsing and then sold.

Over six or seven years, he was the only person left standing as multiple executive committees he worked on were downsized and members retrenched. He investigated senior colleagues and tried to enforce governance standards.

"I became the repository of all the information and shit," he says.

Jeffrey stopped sleeping, his brain fogged, and he felt electricity running through his body. Waking at 2am with his heart pounding, he understands now, was due to cortisol spikes.

"You lose all the enjoyment of life. You are just existing," he says.

He lasted a year in that state before leaving the firm. "I look back and say I did a good job at great cost."

Now 60, Jeffrey says his generation "was taught to endure. Put your head down and don't cause trouble."

"I was always functioning," he says. "I wasn't falling apart."

And anyone reading Lena Dunham's new memoir, Famesick, would recognise that after filming back-to-back seasons of Girls, she was suffering from burnout, among other things.

Dunham's huge success with the TV series, and relentless work ethic (she was a writer, director and star) meant when it was over, she took almost a decade to physically and psychologically recover from the experience.

Lena, Jeffrey and Sylvia are part of a legion of workers whose health has been severely compromised following workplace burnout.

The path to burnout recovery can include mental health leave, seeing a doctor, maybe receiving a diagnosis of anxiety or depression, medicating yourself, and returning to work ready to roll again.

Or — like Jeffrey and Hayley — you could change roles, reduce hours or move into less senior or less stressful positions.

Jeffrey took time off before accepting a contract role with less responsibility.

Hayley took long service, quit her job, sold an investment property to free up cash and took a less stressful (and less well-paid) job as a medical secretary. She has since written a book: Thank You, Burnout.

While taking control of burnout can help recovery, more people are asking if the onus should be on employers.

With almost half of Australian workers feeling burnt out, experts are asking how workplace culture and systems contribute to, or even cause, exhaustion, and whether systemic change might lead to a reduction in burnout overall.

The question of who is responsible for burnout matters. Whether we define burnout as an individual failing or a systemic one determines how we treat it. And, in turn, determines where the responsibility, and the cost, lands.

What is burnout?

Burnout has entered the cultural lexicon with a thoroughness that has outpaced its clinical definition.

It is discussed in podcast episodes and performance reviews, in resignation letters and therapy sessions, on TikTok and in medical journals. Yet despite its ubiquity, or perhaps because of it, there remains no consensus on what burnout actually is and, critically, whose responsibility it is to prevent and treat it.

The World Health Organization classifies burnout as an "occupational phenomenon" in its latest edition of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11), making the definition environmental.

According to the ICD-11, burnout is not a medical condition but a syndrome defined by three dimensions: "exhaustion, increased mental distance or cynicism toward one's job, and reduced professional efficacy." Burnout results from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed.

In short, it is a syndrome caused by work, that affects work performance.

And yet burnout is not included in the latest Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, the DSM-5-TR, which is the primary clinical bible used by doctors, psychologists and insurers in Australia. This has consequences that flow directly into the individual-versus-system debate.

The diagnostic trap

Dr Steven Stolz from the University of Adelaide researches teacher burnout and hosts a podcast on the topic. He has suffered burnout himself.

"From my experience, unless the condition is part of the psychiatric manual, it doesn't exist. Insurers won't recognise burnout," he says. "What happens instead is people take their accrued leave, or [seek a diagnosis of] depression in order to get sick leave."

This pathway comes at a cost. Depression is classified as a disorder of the individual, a medical condition located in the person's brain, body, and history.

When a burned-out worker is diagnosed as depressed, the implied cause shifts from the workplace to the worker. The worker uses their own leave, sees a doctor on their own dime, takes medication, pays for therapy and formulates individual coping strategies.

When they recover, they often return to a workplace unchanged from the one where the injury occurred in the first place.

Matthew Coleshill is an expert in the mental health of professionals at Sydney's Black Dog Institute. He has noticed something interesting: saying you have burnout often carries less stigma than depression.

The word burnout points toward the job, the conditions, the system, rather than inward toward personal pathology.

"If you come up to a colleague and say 'I'm depressed', it's a whole different tone. With burnout, people seem happy to discuss it," he says.

Yet Coleshill believes there is an important, but unexpected, downside to including burnout as a mental health diagnosis: it risks removing responsibility from workplaces.

"When I talk to clinicians about whether burnout should be a diagnosis [in the DSM], they say maybe not," he says. "It becomes an individual thing that you treat, rather than addressing a workplace environment,".

This is the diagnostic trap: the system that would officially recognise burnout in Australia, the DSM, is the same system that would then define burnout as an individual diagnosis.

Once it is classified as an individual vulnerability, the systemic causes can be overlooked. Toxic workplaces stay toxic workplaces. Injured individuals are left to fend for themselves.

The ICD-11 addresses this by placing burnout in its workplace category and referring it to it as a "phenomena" that appears "in the occupational context and should not be applied to describe experiences in other areas of life".

What burnout does to the body

Understanding burnout as a physiological injury, rather than a personal weakness, is itself a political act. It shifts the question from "why can't you cope?" to "what was done to you?"

Burnout occurs when someone feels a level of stress and exhaustion that they can no longer recover from over a weekend or short holiday. It is one of those things that is easy to recognise in retrospect.

Both Hayley and Jeffrey describe their experiences as "frogs in boiling water". Burnout happened almost by stealth. By the time they sought help, they were already feeling the physical effects of stress and prolonged exhaustion.

Burnout also has physiological and neurological components with measurable structural and biochemical markers. It affects brain anatomy, hormonal systems, immune function, cardiovascular health, cellular aging and sleep architecture.

Those who say they cannot think clearly, cannot feel normally, cannot recover with a weekend's rest are not exaggerating. Their brains and bodies have been measurably changed. Burnout puts the body's core stress response system under the hammer.

Under normal conditions, stressors trigger cortisol release, which mobilises energy and sharpens attention before returning to baseline. In chronic burnout, this system becomes dysregulated in measurable ways. Early burnout often shows elevated cortisol: a steroid hormone produced by the adrenal glands that regulates stress response. Advanced burnout frequently shows a flattened, blunted response, as if the system has essentially given up.

Swedish researchers have documented this dysregulation extensively in clinical burnout populations. Because cortisol regulates immune function, inflammation, blood sugar, sleep cycles and cardiovascular function, its dysregulation affects virtually every downstream system in the body.

A landmark Swedish study found people with clinical burnout showed reduced grey matter density in the prefrontal cortex, the brain's centre for executive function, decision-making, emotional regulation and working memory.

The same research found the amygdala, the brain's threat-detection centre, was enlarged in burned-out individuals, with weakened connectivity between the amygdala and the prefrontal cortex. This led to emotional dysregulation and disproportionate reactivity.

Further studies show burnout's impact on sleep, cardiovascular disease, mood and clear thinking.

Yet without clear diagnostic criteria, diagnosing and treating burnout remains difficult.

Valerie, 58, left her public service job in Canberra because of burnout. After a period of increased work pressure, a new boss and the introduction of unfamiliar tasks that had to be performed under time pressure, she couldn't cope.

"I kept staying in the workplace, like a dog returning to vomit," she says. "I went to my boss one day and said I can't keep doing this."

Valerie left. She undertook an external secondment before returning to her original workplace just as COVID-19 hit. "Everything went berserk," she says.

After a COVID-19 infection and working alone at home, Valerie says she was "crying every day".

"I was starting to wake up in the middle of the night, obsessing about work."

Valerie quit her public service job and found a position in the private sector. But the stress continued. She suffered brain fog and forgot instructions as soon as she heard them, resorting to writing everything into notes on her phone.

"I was being a perfectionist. I felt like I barely had time to breathe," she says. "I was sweating, awake all hours, obsessing about things and extremely anxious."

Valerie's symptoms were physical, too: chronically low vitamin D, sky-high levels of bodily inflammation and skin conditions.

After helping to organise a conference she was reprimanded by her boss for appearing disengaged. Valerie spiralled further and her boss suggested time off.

Valerie took early retirement but remains unclear what caused her high levels of stress and illness over the two-year period where "it all fell apart".

Was it burnout or was it something else? She wonders if her perfectionist personality meant she was the cause.

Research shows that Valerie is right to suspect her perfectionism makes her more at risk of burnout.

Longitudinal studies suggest certain personality traits can increase the risk of burnout.

But the data is also clear that, over the long term, personality makes a relatively small impact and workplace culture and expectations are far more significant in determining who burns out.

Workplace wellness

By framing burnout as an individual worker problem, organisations do not have to examine deeper systemic issues like toxic work cultures, unrealistic expectations, or inadequate support structures.

The employee — not the employer — is paying the price.

Kirsty Macdonald, a burnout coach based in London, works with individuals and organisational leadership. She does not mince words.

"Burnout is a collective problem, not an individual problem," Macdonald says. "You don't hear about the bonkers-ness of why this is happening."

So why is this happening?

Macdonald argues society is no longer moving at "a human pace".

"Society is getting faster and faster. People in workplaces designed to make big profits, or workplaces that are poorly staffed, end up running on a treadmill. They can't keep up because they are humans, in a human body and we are not meant to go at such an insane pace all the time."

Noting the crossover of symptoms between burnout and depression, Macdonald wonders if some are prescribed antidepressants when their primary problem is less a chemical imbalance and instead a broken work environment.

"So many people are taking medications to try to fit in with a workplace that is broken," Macdonald says. "They are not broken, it's the workplace."

The medication critique is not about rejecting treatment for people who are genuinely depressed. Antidepressants can be lifesaving. It is questioning whether medicalising a systemic problem shifts both the treatment and the cost onto the individual, while leaving the conditions that caused the harm intact.

South Korean German philosopher Byung-Chul Han argued in his influential 2010 book The Burnout Society that burnout was not a malfunction of the individual psyche but the logical endpoint of a society that had replaced the external prohibitions of the old disciplinary order with an internal compulsion to perform.

The 21st century produces workers who tell themselves there is nothing they cannot achieve. Han argues this is not liberation, but a sophisticated form of oppression. The whip is now held by the self.

In a drive for self-optimisation, excessive positivity and a perfectionist attitude lead to us being both "master and slave".

The exhausted, burned-out worker has not failed to cope with modernity, they have succeeded at it completely, internalising its achievement imperative so thoroughly that they have nothing left to give.

"We owe the cultural achievements of humanity — which include philosophy — to deep, contemplative attention," Han writes. "Culture presumes an environment in which deep attention is possible. Increasingly, such immersive reflection is being displaced by an entirely different form of attention: hyperattention."

'Potato brain'

Jill experienced burnout working at a not-for-profit in Melbourne where she was the only paid staff member. She describes the experience as "potato brain".

"I was showing up, giving signs of life, but nothing useful," she says.

Jill left the organisation but took 18 months to feel recovered.

"In any service work if you are deeply connected to the cause, you are more at risk of burnout," she says.

Jill scoffs at resilience training, mindfulness, wellness programs and apps, as a satisfactory measure to fix burnout.

"The whole idea of someone being resilient is ridiculous," she says. "To whose standard?"

She sees restorative justice as a model for treating burnout. The worker and employer talk about the conditions that lead to burnout and explore new ways of working that may alter the workplace and make it less harmful for others.

The lesson from teachers

The clearest example in Australia of what happens when governments and institutions accept burnout is their problem to solve is in education.

Teacher burnout in Australia is not new. But it has reached a point where its consequences are too visible and too costly to keep attributing to individual teacher inadequacy.

Post-pandemic, we have seen widespread teacher shortages, student underachievement and institutional knowledge walking out the door.

"It's not an individual thing," says Professor Rebecca Collie, from the UNSW School of Education, who has studied burnout in 2,500 Australian teachers.

"Teacher burnout is a system thing that needs to be addressed," she says.

Her research maps the three dimensions of burnout: exhaustion, cynicism (loss of belief in one's ability to make change), and reduced professional efficacy. She found 30–40 per cent of teachers across her samples had been experiencing burnout since prior to the well-documented pressure of teaching during COVID-19 lockdowns.

The numbers are starting to come down but they are still elevated. The reason, she argues, is not because teachers have become more resilient. It is because governments have started to act.

"What's been pleasing is that burnout is going down a little bit because of government efforts to address the teacher shortage and workload," Collie says. "There has been some attention to this issue that wasn't there before. It did reach a point where there was a consequence — teacher shortages — and there has been wider recognition that this is not just an individual problem."

Something had to give.

The National Teacher Workforce Action Plan is a federal government attempt to address burnout on a systemic level. It seeks to do this by reducing workloads, improving retention and increasing teacher support. According to the plan, the key strategies focus on relieving administrative burdens, expanding mentorship and providing financial incentives.

The plan is in its early days, but experts are hopeful it will address some of the conditions that cause teacher burnout.

Dr Ben Arnold, an associate professor in educational leadership at Deakin University, says teachers have higher levels of meaning in their work than many others, but it comes at a cost.

"They have higher workload, higher pace, higher cognitive demands, and very high emotional demands. And then there are all these other non-teaching things as well," he says.

These include communication with parents that goes way beyond the usual check-in at parent-teacher night, a greater amount of admin and external testing.

"Teachers often describe earlier decades in Australian education as a period when they experienced greater professional autonomy and public trust," says Arnold, whose research focuses on how education policies and working conditions in schools impact the health, sustainability and diversity of teachers.

Increasing emphasis on performance measurement, accountability, external testing and compliance has introduced additional pressures and administrative demands, he says, and teacher goodwill holds the system together.

"A strong sense of public service and commitment to students is often what keeps school systems functioning under pressure, but it can also make teachers particularly vulnerable to burnout when workloads and expectations become unsustainable," he says.

The lesson from education is not to wait until staffing crises become impossible to ignore. It is that when institutions accept responsibility, when they stop treating burnout as a problem with employees and start treating it as a problem of working conditions, the numbers move.

"We see there's a link between teacher burnout and student achievement," says Collie. "It is a system thing."

A policy landscape catching up

Australia has begun to build a legal framework that places some of the burden of prevention back on employers. But it's uneven.

The right to disconnect, enacted in August 2024 for businesses with more than 15 employees, protects workers who refuse to respond to work communications outside working hours.

The legislation was criticised by some. The Business Council of Australia described it as a threat to productivity and competitiveness. The previous opposition committed to repealing it.

Yet a 2022 Australia Institute survey found only 9 per cent of respondents believed such a policy would not positively affect their lives.

More significant are the reforms to Work Health and Safety Regulations requiring employers to proactively manage psychosocial risk.

In 2023, Court Services Victoria was prosecuted and fined $379,157 for failing to manage psychological wellbeing risks, following what was described as a toxic culture within the Coroners Court.

Ben Arnold notes these legislative developments are meaningful but incomplete.

"Government, WorkSafe and the regulators have recognised the issues," he says. "The sticking point now is: what are employers actually doing about it?"

Workers' compensation schemes complicate the picture further.

"All of the state compensation schemes have blown out and it should be that the schemes are funded by employers," Arnold argues. "But there's not yet a definitive risk assessment of what constitutes a workplace where burnout is likely to occur."

He adds: "Psychological injury claims have increased significantly and those claims are often complex and costly. While burnout itself is not usually treated as a compensable condition, workplace psychosocial hazards clearly contribute to burnout and other psychological injuries."

The limits of individual solutions

None of this means individual action is pointless. Stolz identifies perfectionism, where self-worth is entirely tied to professional performance, as an internal risk factor that no amount of workplace reform will address alone.

"It's not one over the other [perfectionism and workplace culture]," he says. "They are both contributing factors."

But he says that individual coping strategies have a ceiling.

"Mindfulness, taking time off: these can keep burnout at bay. But if you are working in a toxic workplace, you need to address that," he says. "Leaving one toxic workplace for another will not help."

Hayley Hughes, who said yes to everything, believes her burnout was a type of anxiety: "My burnout was on me. Nobody is at fault, it's because of me. For many years I was a perfectionist, a people-pleaser."

Since restructuring her relationship to work by refusing to let it define her sense of self and reducing her hours, Hayley says she has learned to read her own warning signs.

"It forced me to disconnect my identity from my job," she says.

Jeffrey, years after his crisis, has built personal practices that he credits with preventing a recurrence: no alcohol, time in nature, careful attention to sleep.

"I'm much better able to recognise and act," he says.

But both acknowledge their recoveries depended on having something most burned-out workers do not — the economic cushion to make those choices.

Hayley sold an investment. Jeffrey was able to switch roles and take time off in between.

The cleanest individual solutions to burnout — leave the job, take months off, downshift — are available only to those with financial security.

For everyone else, the question of systemic change is not a luxury. It's the only real option.

Words: Brigid Delaney
